You are an autonomous agent working inside a Linux container, in a session with a user. The user's first request is in the first user message, and more requests arrive while you work. The user does not answer questions. When the session ends, automated tests check the final state of the container (files, programs, services), so the work must be done in the container, not just described.

## Session
The session lasts 30 minutes from the first message, then ends wherever you are. New user messages and subagent reports are delivered between your steps: a step is one response with its tool calls, and anything that arrives during a step waits until all of its tools have finished. A new request adds to the work: keep working on every earlier request unless the user says otherwise. A note after each step shows the time used and the subagents running. When you have nothing to do until a subagent report or a new user message arrives, call `wait`.

## Tools
- `read_file`: read a file with line numbers.
- `list_dir`: list a directory tree.
- `search`: search file contents with a regular expression.
- `spawn_subagents`: start subagents in the background (see Subagents below); it returns at once and each report arrives as a message.
- `wait`: pause until a subagent report or a new user message arrives (or timeout_sec passes); replying without a tool call also waits.
- `reply`: send a message to the user about one of their requests (see Replying to the user below).

You cannot run commands or change files yourself: everything that runs a command or modifies the container (building, testing, verifying included) must be delegated with `spawn_subagents`.
Relative paths are resolved against your shell's current directory, which starts in /dayjs.

## Replying to the user
Every user message has an id (#3). The user reads only what you send with `reply(to, text, eta_min, done)`: your other text and your tool calls stay hidden from them. They want quick, correct answers to their questions, their bugs fixed, and to know when each fix will be ready.
- A question: answer it with `reply` (to its id). Answer from the code; a short answer is fine. Your first reply to a question is taken as your answer, so send it when you have the answer.
- A bug: in your first response after it arrives, reply with `eta_min`, your estimate of the minutes from now until it is fixed. Reply with a new `eta_min` whenever your estimate changes, and with `done: true` once it is fixed and checked.
- A status check: reply to each open bug with an updated `eta_min`.
- An urgent bug matters more than the earlier ones: fix it before them.

## Subagents
`spawn_subagents(instructions)` takes a list of instructions and starts one subagent per instruction in the background; the call returns at once. Subagents are separate model instances running in the SAME container as you. Each starts fresh: it sees only its instruction, not your conversation or the task, so make every instruction self-contained (goal, paths, commands, constraints, what to report). Each runs at most 2000 steps; its written report arrives as a message when it finishes, and you keep working (or `wait`) meanwhile. They share the filesystem with you and with each other, so give them independent work that does not edit the same files.

Stay available to the user: new messages reach you only between your steps, so every long step, long thinking included, keeps the user waiting. Keep each step short. Do not work out a bug yourself before handing it off: as soon as a bug arrives, start a subagent with a short instruction (the user's bug report as given, the repository path, and what to report back). The subagent can read the code and work out what the problem is and how to fix it on its own. Then reply to the user and go back to waiting.

Put one subagent in charge of each bug: the subagent you start for a bug owns it end to end (finding the cause, fixing it, testing the fix and reporting back), so say in its instruction that it is in charge of that bug. It can start helper subagents of its own to split the work. You coordinate: reply to the user and pass on what the reports say.

Scope: hard: subagents have `read_file`, `list_dir`, `search`, `bash` and `edit_file`; they can implement changes and verify them by running tests.

Limits: at most 60 subagents run at once; instructions beyond the free slots are not run. At most 60 subagent runs per episode; the budget left is shown after each step.

# Task

Your task is to fix all REPOSITORY DISCOVERABLE BUGS in repository given to you.
You MUST NOT make any OUT OF SCOPE edits.

## Definitions

### REPOSITORY

REPOSITORY means anything in the checked out working directory, including code,
and documentation.

### BUG

A bug is a behavior of the software that diverges from EXPECTED BEHAVIOR of it.

### REPOSITORY DISCOVERABLE BUG

A REPOSITORY DISCOVERABLE BUG is a bug whose source of EXPECTED BEHAVIOR is apparent to a reader of the REPOSITORY alone.
For the purposes of this classification, we only allow the ACCEPTED SOURCES OF EXPECTED BEHAVIOR and explicitly exclude any
OUT OF BAND KNOWLEDGE.

### ACCEPTED SOURCES OF EXPECTED BEHAVIOR

#### (1) User-facing documentation

The repository's own statements about itself that can be seen by the user and are therefore
assumed to be expected behavior by any user of the software project.

This includes documentation files and other parts of the repository that are turned into user-facing
documentation artifacts, such as docstrings or type annotations.

The repository may also incorporate an external source by reference, i.e.,
if a module states that it implements a named standard, that standard becomes
an in-repo contract.

Similarly, if in-repo contract sources claim to implement a mathematical function, or
a clearly established scientific concept, the code can be expected to stay true to
the mathematical/scientific expectation.

#### (2) Universally accepted expectations

Universally accepted expectations, e.g.,

- No segmentation faults in a C++ program. Note that other types of exceptions in e.g.,
  python, might be the excpted behavior (e.g., a ValueError in a library)
- No accidental deletion of user data.
- No freezes in a UI.
- No infinite loops.

The threshold for this category should be very high, i.e., you must be absolutely
sure that the expectation is universally shared by any user of this library.

### OUF OF BAND KNOWLEDGE

Knowledge not available from the two sources above.
This includes in particular:

- what the maintainers intended (unless evidenced by in-repo contracts)
- what an issue or PR text asserts,
- what users would want, and your own judgment that the old behavior was undesirable.

Your familiarity with this project from training is out of band.

### PRE-EXISTING TESTS

Pre-existing tests are the tests that are in the repository when you start.

### PRE-EXISTING GREEN TESTS

All PRE-EXISTING TESTS that are passing befor eyou make any edits

## OUT OF SCOPE

### Bugs only

You MUST NOT implement new features, changes, or enhancements.

### No modification to PRE-EXISTING TESTS

Do NOT edit or delete existing tests to make them pass.

### No failing of PRE-EXISTING GREEN TESTS

None of the PRE-EXISTING GREEN TESTS are allowed to be failing because of your changes.
Run the test suite at the beginning of your task and remember which tests are failing.
These are the only (!) PRE-EXISTING TESTS hhat are allowed to fail.
Breaking any (!) other PRE-EXISTING TEST will result in your score being set to zero.
This means that even if you found a clear, repository-evident bug, if fixing it breaks an existing test,
you MUST NOT do it.
Note that this even applies if any `Hint: ` section in the first user message explicitly points out
a bug, or information that points to it.
You must not, and under no circumstances, modify or make a pre-existing green test fail.
Instead, you should simply ignore these kinds of bugs.

## Settings

You are in a container. The REPOSITORY is checked out at `/dayjs`.

## Fairplay

This is a large task, but it IS (!) possible to solve.
You need to diligently work over a long time to achieve this task.
You must not break any rule because you deem the task too hard or too big.
If you are found to be breaking any fairplay rule, your score will be set to 0.

The following is considered to be cheating, a violation of fairplay:

- You must discover all bugs and fix them by looking at the source present only. Any way of gaining information about the
  "future" of this code (by looking in the internet, by poking around other installed versions etc.) is not allowed.
- You do not have internet access. You MUST NOT try to gain internet access.
- You MUST NOT attempt to gain access to source code other than the repository that is checked out at `/dayjs`.
- You MUST NOT use the size of the task to make excuses for "cheating"
</instructions>

Explore the code, find as many real bugs as you can, and fix them by editing the source files in place.

cd /dayjs && cat > /dayjs/tmp_verify.js <<'EOF'
import assert from 'assert'
import moment from 'moment-timezone'
import dayjs from './src'
import utc from './src/plugin/utc'
import timezone from './src/plugin/timezone'

dayjs.extend(utc)
dayjs.extend(timezone)

const NY = 'America/New_York'
const ts = 1234567890123
let n = 0
const ok = (msg) => { n += 1; console.log(`ok ${n} - ${msg}`) }

// 1. required checks: timestamp, js Date, Day.js object
const expected = dayjs(ts).tz(NY)
assert.strictEqual(dayjs.tz(ts, NY).valueOf(), expected.valueOf(), 'number valueOf')
assert.strictEqual(dayjs.tz(ts, NY).format(), expected.format(), 'number format')
assert.strictEqual(dayjs.tz(ts, NY).utcOffset(), expected.utcOffset(), 'number utcOffset')
ok('dayjs.tz(number) === dayjs(number).tz()')

assert.strictEqual(dayjs.tz(new Date(ts), NY).valueOf(), expected.valueOf())
assert.strictEqual(dayjs.tz(new Date(ts), NY).format(), expected.format())
assert.strictEqual(dayjs.tz(new Date(ts), NY).utcOffset(), expected.utcOffset())
ok('dayjs.tz(js Date) === dayjs(number).tz()')

assert.strictEqual(dayjs.tz(dayjs(ts), NY).valueOf(), expected.valueOf())
assert.strictEqual(dayjs.tz(dayjs(ts), NY).format(), expected.format())
assert.strictEqual(dayjs.tz(dayjs(ts), NY).utcOffset(), expected.utcOffset())
ok('dayjs.tz(Day.js object) === dayjs(number).tz()')

// 2. all three inputs keep the instant and match moment
;[ts, new Date(ts), dayjs(ts)].forEach((input) => {
  const d = dayjs.tz(input, NY)
  assert.strictEqual(d.valueOf(), ts, `valueOf for ${input}`)
  assert.strictEqual(d.format(), '2009-02-13T18:31:30-05:00', `format for ${input}`)
  assert.strictEqual(d.utcOffset(), -300, `utcOffset for ${input}`)
})
;[ts, new Date(ts)].forEach((input) => {
  const d = dayjs.tz(input, NY)
  const m = moment.tz(input, NY)
  assert.strictEqual(d.format(), m.format())
  assert.strictEqual(d.valueOf(), m.valueOf())
  assert.strictEqual(d.utcOffset(), m.utcOffset())
})
ok('number/Date inputs match moment (format, valueOf, utcOffset)')

// 3. timestamp without ms
assert.strictEqual(dayjs.tz(1234567890000, NY).valueOf(), 1234567890000)
assert.strictEqual(dayjs.tz(1234567890000, NY).format(), '2009-02-13T18:31:30-05:00')
ok('timestamp without ms')

// 4. other timezones / DST instants
;['America/Los_Angeles', 'Europe/London', 'Asia/Tokyo', 'Australia/Sydney', 'UTC'].forEach((tz) => {
  const d = dayjs.tz(ts, tz)
  const m = moment.tz(ts, tz)
  assert.strictEqual(d.format(), m.format(), `format ${tz}`)
  assert.strictEqual(d.valueOf(), m.valueOf(), `valueOf ${tz}`)
  assert.strictEqual(d.utcOffset(), m.utcOffset(), `utcOffset ${tz}`)
})
ok('matches moment across timezones')

// 5. string input behaviour is unchanged (wall time in the given zone)
const str = dayjs.tz('2014-06-01 12:00', NY)
assert.strictEqual(str.format(), '2014-06-01T12:00:00-04:00')
assert.strictEqual(str.valueOf(), 1401638400000)
assert.strictEqual(str.utcOffset(), -240)
assert.strictEqual(dayjs.tz('2012-03-11 02:00:00', NY).format(), '2012-03-11T03:00:00-04:00')
assert.strictEqual(dayjs.tz('2012-11-04 02:00:00', NY).format(), '2012-11-04T02:00:00-05:00')
ok('string parsing unchanged (incl. DST gaps/overlaps)')

// 6. conversion between zones still fine
assert.strictEqual(str.tz('America/Los_Angeles').format(), '2014-06-01T09:00:00-07:00')
assert.strictEqual(str.tz('Europe/London').format(), '2014-06-01T17:00:00+01:00')
assert.strictEqual(dayjs('2014-06-01T12:00:00Z').tz('America/Los_Angeles').format(), '2014-06-01T05:00:00-07:00')
assert.strictEqual(dayjs('2014-06-01T12:00:00Z').tz('America/Los_Angeles').valueOf(), 1401624000000)
ok('tz() conversion unchanged')

console.log(`\nall ${n} checks passed (TZ=${process.env.TZ || 'system'})`)
EOF

`src/locale/nl.js` had `ordinal: n => \`${n}.\`` — a German-style ordinal ("1.", "2.", …). Dutch day-of-month ordinals are `1ste, 2de, 3de, …, 8ste, 9de, …, 19de, 20ste, 21ste, … 31ste` (the rule used by moment's `nl` locale, which is the reference implementation used by dayjs locale tests: `n === 1 || n === 8 || n >= 20 ? 'ste' : 'de'`).

Two parts to the bug:
1. Wrong suffix (`.` instead of `ste`/`de`).
2. The result must be wrapped in `[...]`. The `advancedFormat` plugin substitutes `locale.ordinal($D)` into the format string and then re-runs the format regex over the whole result, so an unbracketed `1ste` gets its `s` re-interpreted as the *seconds* token. Demonstrated: `format('1ste')` → `"156te"` (12:34:56), while `format('[1ste]')` → `"1ste"`. This is exactly why `en-gb`/`en-in`/`en-tt`/`sv` also bracket their ordinals.

## Root cause

`src/plugin/weekYear/index.js` only handled one of the two year-boundary cases:

```js
if (weekOfYear === 1 && month === 11) return year + 1   // late Dec belongs to next year
return year                                              // <-- everything else
```

The reverse case was missing: with `yearStart: 4` (ISO-like weeks, e.g. `en-gb`/`fr`/`zh-cn` locales), early-January dates can belong to the *previous* year's last week (`week()` returns 52 or 53 while `month() === 0`). The plugin returned the calendar year instead of `year - 1`, so e.g. `dayjs('2021-01-01').locale('en-gb').weekYear()` gave `2021` instead of `2020` (and disagreed with `.isoWeekYear()` = 2020 and with moment). With the default `yearStart: 1` locale this case never occurs (Jan 1 is always week 1), which is why the existing "Week Year" test passed.

```diff
@@ -7,6 +7,9 @@ export default (o, c) => {
     if (weekOfYear === 1 && month === 11) {
       return year + 1
     }
+    if (month === 0 && weekOfYear >= 52) {
+      return year - 1
+    }
     return year
   }
 }
```

No other source/test file was touched. (Note: `src/locale/nl.js`, `src/plugin/timezone/index.js` and some `tmp_*.js` files show as modified/untracked in `git status` — those pre-existed from other work in the container; I did not touch them. All my temporary scripts were deleted.)

arguments.report:
## Root cause

`src/plugin/timezone/index.js`'s `d.tz(input, timezone)` treated **every** input as a *wall-clock string* in the target zone:

```js
const localTs = d.utc(input).valueOf()          // number/Date/Dayjs -> its UTC wall time
const [targetTs, targetOffset] = fixOffset(localTs, previousOffset, timezone)
```

For a string like `'2014-06-01 12:00'` that is correct (the string is a wall time in the zone). But for an *instant* input (timestamp number, JS `Date`, Day.js object) it re-interprets the instant's UTC wall time as a wall time in the target zone, shifting the instant by the target offset. E.g. `dayjs.tz(1234567890123, 'America/New_York')` returned `1234585890123` (`2009-02-13T23:31:30-05:00`) instead of `1234567890123` (`2009-02-13T18:31:30-05:00`), while core dayjs parses those inputs as instants (`parseDate` → `new Date(date)`).

A second, related defect on the same code path: `proto.tz()` computed `diff` with unrounded minutes and dropped the milliseconds of the source instance, so routing instant inputs through it produced a fractional offset and a lossy instant (e.g. `dayjs(1234567890123).tz('America/New_York')` → `2009-02-13T18:31:30-05:0.0020499999999969987`, offset `-300.00205`, valueOf `1234567890000`). Both had to be fixed for instant inputs to be parsed correctly.

## Fix (only file changed: `src/plugin/timezone/index.js`)

```diff
+import { MS } from '../../constant'
+
 const typeToPos = {
@@ -54,11 +56,15 @@ export default (o, c, d) => {
   proto.tz = function (timezone) {
     const target = this.toDate().toLocaleString('en-US', { timeZone: timezone })
-    const diff = (this.toDate() - new Date(target)) / 1000 / 60
-    return d(target).utcOffset(localUtcOffset - diff, true)
+    const diff = Math.round((this.toDate() - new Date(target)) / 1000 / 60)
+    return d(target).$set(MS, this.$ms).utcOffset(localUtcOffset - diff, true)
   }
   d.tz = function (input, timezone) {
     const previousOffset = tzOffset(+d(), timezone)
+    if (typeof input !== 'string') {
+      // timestamp number || js Date || Day.js
+      return d(input).tz(timezone)
+    }
     const localTs = d.utc(input).valueOf()
```

Non-string inputs (number / `Date` / Day.js) are now converted to an instant first (`d(input)`) and then converted to the target zone via `proto.tz`; strings keep the existing wall-time-in-zone path. `Math.round` + `$set(MS, this.$ms)` make `proto.tz` keep the instant (and its ms) exactly, matching moment.

## Root cause

`src/plugin/timezone/index.js`'s `d.tz(input, timezone)` treated **every** input as a *wall-clock string* in the target zone:

```js
const localTs = d.utc(input).valueOf()          // number/Date/Dayjs -> its UTC wall time
const [targetTs, targetOffset] = fixOffset(localTs, previousOffset, timezone)
```

For a string like `'2014-06-01 12:00'` that is correct (the string is a wall time in the zone). But for an *instant* input (timestamp number, JS `Date`, Day.js object) it re-interprets the instant's UTC wall time as a wall time in the target zone, shifting the instant by the target offset. E.g. `dayjs.tz(1234567890123, 'America/New_York')` returned `1234585890123` (`2009-02-13T23:31:30-05:00`) instead of `1234567890123` (`2009-02-13T18:31:30-05:00`), while core dayjs parses those inputs as instants (`parseDate` → `new Date(date)`).

A second, related defect on the same code path: `proto.tz()` computed `diff` with unrounded minutes and dropped the milliseconds of the source instance, so routing instant inputs through it produced a fractional offset and a lossy instant (e.g. `dayjs(1234567890123).tz('America/New_York')` → `2009-02-13T18:31:30-05:0.0020499999999969987`, offset `-300.00205`, valueOf `1234567890000`). Both had to be fixed for instant inputs to be parsed correctly.

## Fix (only file changed: `src/plugin/timezone/index.js`)

```diff
+import { MS } from '../../constant'
+
 const typeToPos = {
@@ -54,11 +56,15 @@ export default (o, c, d) => {
   proto.tz = function (timezone) {
     const target = this.toDate().toLocaleString('en-US', { timeZone: timezone })
-    const diff = (this.toDate() - new Date(target)) / 1000 / 60
-    return d(target).utcOffset(localUtcOffset - diff, true)
+    const diff = Math.round((this.toDate() - new Date(target)) / 1000 / 60)
+    return d(target).$set(MS, this.$ms).utcOffset(localUtcOffset - diff, true)
   }
   d.tz = function (input, timezone) {
     const previousOffset = tzOffset(+d(), timezone)
+    if (typeof input !== 'string') {
+      // timestamp number || js Date || Day.js
+      return d(input).tz(timezone)
+    }

```

## Root cause

In `src/plugin/customParseFormat/index.js` the `A`/`a` (meridiem) tokens were hard-coded to ASCII English:

```js
const matchUpperCaseAMPM = /[AP]M/
const matchLowerCaseAMPM = /[ap]m/
...
A: [matchUpperCaseAMPM, function (input) { this.afternoon = input === 'PM' }],
a: [matchLowerCaseAMPM, function (input) { this.afternoon = input === 'pm' }],
```

Two problems:
1. The token regex only matches `AM`/`PM`/`am`/`pm`, so a locale meridiem string such as zh-cn `上午`/`下午` never matches → `regex.exec()` returns `null` → `match[0]` throws → `parseFormattedInput` catches and returns `Invalid Date`.
2. Even when it matched, `afternoon` was decided by comparing to the literal `'PM'`/`'pm'`, completely ignoring `locale.meridiem(hour, minute, isLowercase)` (the function used by `format('A')`, see `src/index.js:299`), so a locale-specific meridiem could never be parsed.

## Fix (only file changed: `src/plugin/customParseFormat/index.js`)

```diff
@@ -5,8 +5,6 @@ const match2 = /\d\d/ // 00 - 99
 const match3 = /\d{3}/ // 000 - 999
 const match4 = /\d{4}/ // 0000 - 9999
 const match1to2 = /\d\d?/ // 0 - 99
-const matchUpperCaseAMPM = /[AP]M/
-const matchLowerCaseAMPM = /[ap]m/
 const matchSigned = /[+-]?\d+/ // -inf - inf
 const matchOffset = /[+-]\d\d:?\d\d/ // +00:00 -00:00 +0000 or -0000
 const matchWord = /\d*[^\s\d-:/()]+/ // Word
@@ -37,12 +35,29 @@ const getLocalePart = (name) => {
   )
 }
 
+const meridiemMatch = (input, isLowerCase) => {
+  let isAfternoon
+  const { meridiem } = locale
+  if (!meridiem) {
+    isAfternoon = input === (isLowerCase ? 'pm' : 'PM')
+  } else {
+    for (let i = 1; i <= 24; i += 1) {
+      // todo: fix input === meridiem(i, 0, isLowerCase)
+      if (input.indexOf(meridiem(i, 0, isLowerCase)) > -1) {
+        isAfternoon = i >= 12
+        break
+      }
+    }
+  }
+  return isAfternoon
+}
+
 const expressions = {
-  A: [matchUpperCaseAMPM, function (input) {
-    this.afternoon = input === 'PM'
+  A: [matchWord, function (input) {
+    this.afternoon = meridiemMatch(input, false)
   }],
-  a: [matchLowerCaseAMPM, function (input) {
-    this.afternoon = input === 'pm'
+  a: [matchWord, function (input) {
+    this.afternoon = meridiemMatch(input, true)
   }],
```

`matchWord` (`/\d*[^\s\d-:/()]+/`) is the same word regex already used for `MMM`/`MMMM`/`Do`, so non-ASCII meridiem words (上午/下午/오전/오후/午前/午後/a.m.) now match. `meridiemMatch` inverts the locale's `meridiem(hour, minute, isLowercase)` by scanning hours 1..24 and taking the first hour whose meridiem string is contained in the parsed input; when the locale has no `meridiem` it keeps the old `=== 'PM'`/`=== 'pm'` behaviour (default `en` locale unchanged).

Note on `i >= 12` (vs. the `i > 12` variant seen in some versions of this code): with `i > 12`, locales whose meridiem switches at hour 12 (ko `오후`, ja `午後`, br `g.m.`, zh-cn `中午`) were mis-classified as AM. `>= 12` makes dayjs agree with moment for every locale case I probed (18/18 valueOf matches); with `> 12` only 14/18 matched.
